intents: make something that is already good even better
add a small touch that brings out the best in something, like salt in a soup or a frame round a painting
raise the quality or value of something, such as your CV or your chances
ru_cue: сделать хорошее еще лучше, добавить ему ценности

upgrades.plain: A squeeze of lemon will really [make the flavour better].
upgrades.better: A squeeze of lemon will really *enhance* the flavour.

upgrades.plain: She's doing an evening course to [improve] her chances of getting promoted.
upgrades.better: She's doing an evening course to *enhance* her chances of getting promoted.

upgrades.plain: My sister's wedding photos looked flat, so I stayed up till 2 a.m. trying to [make the colours better] before she saw them.
upgrades.better: My sister's wedding photos looked flat, so I stayed up till 2 a.m. trying to *enhance* the colours before she saw them.

nuance: For adding to something already good or neutral; to fix something bad, say improve: you enhance a flavour, you don't enhance a disaster.
personal: What one small change would most enhance your daily routine?
Who do you know who enhances any party just by turning up?
hook: Sounds like 'in hands': in a good chef's hands, a fine dish becomes even better.

intents: a deep feeling of care for someone who is suffering, together with the wish to help
what a good nurse shows a frightened patient, even at the end of a long shift
the warm feeling that makes you stop for someone in pain instead of walking past
ru_cue: сердечное участие к тому, кому плохо, и желание помочь

upgrades.plain: The doctor gave us the bad news with real [kindness and care].
upgrades.better: The doctor gave us the bad news with real *compassion*.

upgrades.plain: I'd failed my driving test for the third time, and my instructor treated me with [kindness] instead of lecturing me.
upgrades.better: I'd failed my driving test for the third time, and my instructor treated me with *compassion* instead of lecturing me.

upgrades.plain: We need managers who show some [kindness towards] people who are struggling.
upgrades.better: We need managers who show some *compassion* for people who are struggling.

collocations.frame: show ___ for those who are suffering

ru_trap: Russian 'сострадание к' tempts 'compassion to'; English says compassion *for* (or towards) someone.
nuance: Stronger than sympathy: you are moved by someone's suffering and want to help, not just sorry for them.
personal: When did someone's compassion make a hard day easier for you?
Who in your family shows the most compassion to strangers?
hook: Com-PASSION: 'with passion' for helping someone in pain.

intents: do your best work under pressure, as if the stress gives you energy
when deadlines, crowds or competition make you better instead of wearing you out
need something hard or hectic in order to feel alive and do well
ru_cue: черпать силы именно в том, что другим тяжело, и расцветать от этого

upgrades.plain: Some people [do really well under] pressure; I just panic.
upgrades.better: Some people *thrive on* pressure; I just panic.

upgrades.plain: My dad [gets his energy from] arguments at dinner, which drives my mum mad.
upgrades.better: My dad *thrives on* arguments at dinner, which drives my mum mad.

upgrades.plain: Small cafes [do well because of] their regulars.
upgrades.better: Small cafes *thrive on* their regulars.

ru_trap: Russian 'благодаря' tempts 'thrive thanks to' or 'thrive from'; English says thrive *on* something.
nuance: What you thrive on is usually something others find hard (pressure, chaos); flourish just means grow well in good conditions.
personal: What kind of pressure do you thrive on, and what kind breaks you?
Who do you know who seems to thrive on chaos?
hook: 'Thrive' sounds like 'драйв': she gets her драйв from pressure.

intents: the strong effect that one thing has on another
how much a change really changed people's lives, for better or worse
the mark a good teacher leaves on a child for years afterwards
ru_cue: сильное воздействие, заметный след, который что-то оставляет

upgrades.plain: Rising rents have had a big [effect] on young people.
upgrades.better: Rising rents have had a big *impact* on young people.

upgrades.plain: Losing the contract had a serious [effect] on the whole team, and two people lost their jobs.
upgrades.better: Losing the contract had a serious *impact* on the whole team, and two people lost their jobs.

upgrades.plain: The new manager [made a big difference] in her first month: sales went up by a third.
upgrades.better: The new manager made a big *impact* in her first month: sales went up by a third.

ru_trap: Russian 'оказать влияние' tempts 'render an impact'; English says *have* (or make) an impact *on* something.
nuance: Stronger and more noticeable than effect; in IELTS writing 'have an impact on' is safe, while 'impact' as a verb sounds like business jargon.
personal: What decision has had the biggest impact on your life so far?
Which teacher had the biggest impact on you, and how?
gesture: Punch a fist into your open palm: thud.
hook: Im-PACT: picture a tightly packed snowball smacking a window and leaving a mark.

intents: a promise to keep giving your time and effort to something
what a puppy really is: a ten-year promise, not a weekend idea
the steady dedication of someone who trains every morning for years
ru_cue: обещание и готовность годами вкладывать в дело время и силы

upgrades.plain: Getting a dog is a huge [responsibility that lasts for years].
upgrades.better: Getting a dog is a huge *commitment*.

upgrades.plain: I can't [promise anything] until I've seen my work schedule.
upgrades.better: I can't make a *commitment* until I've seen my work schedule.

upgrades.plain: My mum drove me to swimming at six every morning for ten years; that's real [dedication].
upgrades.better: My mum drove me to swimming at six every morning for ten years; that's real *commitment*.

ru_trap: Russian 'взять обязательство' tempts 'take a commitment'; English says *make* a commitment, and 'commitment to doing', not 'to do'.
nuance: A commitment ties you to something over time, while a promise can be a one-off; plural 'commitments' means the things that fill your time.
personal: What is the biggest commitment you have ever made?
Who do you know whose commitment to a hobby or job you admire?
hook: 'Commit' sounds like 'комитет': you promised the committee you'd come every Monday for years.

intents: be forced to leave university because your grades were too bad
when you miss so many exams that the college throws you out
fail so badly that you're no longer allowed to stay on the course
ru_cue: вылететь из вуза, потому что завалил экзамены
plain: fail and get kicked out of

upgrades.plain: He played video games all year and [got kicked out of university for failing].
upgrades.better: He played video games all year and *flunked out of* university.

upgrades.plain: I was terrified I'd [fail and get thrown out of] medical school and have to tell my parents.
upgrades.better: I was terrified I'd *flunk out of* medical school and have to tell my parents.

upgrades.plain: You won't [get thrown out of] the course for one bad essay.
upgrades.better: You won't *flunk out of* the course for one bad essay.

ru_trap: 'Flunk an exam' means fail one exam; leaving the university is 'flunk *out of*', never 'flunk from'.
nuance: Informal. You drop out by choice; you flunk out because your grades forced you to leave.
personal: Did you ever worry you might flunk out of a course? Which one?
Do you know anyone who flunked out of university and then did well anyway?
gesture: Jerk your thumb over your shoulder, like a bouncer throwing someone out of the door.
hook: 'Flunk' sounds like 'плюнь': плюнь на учебу, и вылетишь из университета.

intents: introduce the opposite case: what's true for one side is reversed for the other
my brother loves the cold; I, the other way round, want somewhere hot
a formal way to flip a comparison and look at it from the reverse side
ru_cue: а у другой стороны все ровно наоборот

upgrades.plain: Prices in the city keep rising; [on the other hand], village houses are getting cheaper.
upgrades.better: Prices in the city keep rising; *conversely*, village houses are getting cheaper.

upgrades.plain: He talks non-stop when he's nervous. [On the other hand], I go completely silent, which made our first date very awkward.
upgrades.better: He talks non-stop when he's nervous. *Conversely*, I go completely silent, which made our first date very awkward.

upgrades.plain: Some plants need full sun. [In contrast], ferns like deep shade.
upgrades.better: Some plants need full sun. *Conversely*, ferns like deep shade.

collocations.frame: Stress causes poor sleep and, ___, poor sleep causes stress.
Sales rose in the north. ___, they fell in the south.

ru_trap: Russian 'наоборот' also means 'quite the opposite!' when you contradict someone; *conversely* only compares two cases and never contradicts.
nuance: Use it when two sides mirror each other (A rises, B falls); for a simple contrast or a different point, 'however' or 'on the other hand' is enough.
personal: What gives you energy, and what, conversely, drains you?
Think of a family member who is your opposite: what do you love that they, conversely, can't stand?
gesture: Hold one hand palm up, then flip it palm down: the other way round.
hook: ConVERSEly rhymes with 'reverse-ly': the same picture, reversed.

intents: you could reasonably claim this, though some people would disagree
when you call something the best ever but leave room for others to think differently
a careful way to make a bold claim without sounding too sure of yourself
ru_cue: пожалуй, можно смело сказать, хотя не все согласятся

upgrades.plain: This is [probably] the best album they ever made, but my brother would fight me on that.
upgrades.better: This is *arguably* the best album they ever made, but my brother would fight me on that.

upgrades.plain: Rain was, [I'd say], the main reason the crop failed.
upgrades.better: Rain was *arguably* the main reason the crop failed.

upgrades.plain: Mobile phones are [maybe] the most important invention of the last fifty years.
upgrades.better: Mobile phones are *arguably* the most important invention of the last fifty years.

collocations.frame: ___ the best player of her generation
___ the most important invention of the century

ru_trap: Not 'аргументированно' (with arguments): *arguably* means 'one could say', and it supports the claim rather than doubting it.
nuance: It leans towards agreeing with the claim: it softens a strong statement, usually a superlative, rather than casting doubt on it.
personal: What is arguably the best decision you have ever made?
Who is arguably the funniest person in your family?
hook: Arguably = 'argue-ably': you can say it, but someone could argue back.

intents: a formal way to say 'in spite of' before a noun, such as the weather or the cost
the plan went ahead even though there was an obstacle in the way
this problem existed, but it didn't change the outcome (official, written style)
ru_cue: вопреки помехе, которая могла бы все испортить

upgrades.plain: [Despite] the terrible weather, the team played brilliantly.
upgrades.better: *Notwithstanding* the terrible weather, the team played brilliantly.

upgrades.plain: She took the job [in spite of] the two-hour commute, and her kids hardly saw her that year.
upgrades.better: She took the job *notwithstanding* the two-hour commute, and her kids hardly saw her that year.

upgrades.plain: [Despite] a slow start, the book sold well.
upgrades.better: *Notwithstanding* a slow start, the book sold well.

collocations.frame: These difficulties ___, the project was a success.

nuance: Formal and mostly written, and it can follow its noun ('these problems notwithstanding'); in speech, despite sounds more natural.
personal: What did you once achieve notwithstanding a serious obstacle?
Who do you know who stays cheerful notwithstanding real hardship?
hook: 'Not-with-standing': the rain was there, but it was not standing in our way.

intents: add a small reservation to something positive: good, though a little expensive
a short 'although' followed by just an adjective or adverb, with no verb
admit a weak point in passing: he agreed, but not happily
ru_cue: с маленькой оговоркой: хорошо, но не без минуса

upgrades.plain: The flat is lovely, [though it's] a bit small for two.
upgrades.better: The flat is lovely, *albeit* a bit small for two.

upgrades.plain: He agreed to come to my brother's wedding, [but he wasn't happy about it].
upgrades.better: He agreed to come to my brother's wedding, *albeit* reluctantly.

upgrades.plain: Sales improved, [although] more slowly than we'd hoped.
upgrades.better: Sales improved, *albeit* more slowly than we'd hoped.

ru_trap: Russian 'хотя' starts a full clause; *albeit* takes no verb: 'albeit slowly', never 'albeit it was slow'.
nuance: Shorter and more formal than although: it adds a quick qualifier to a word or phrase, never a full clause with its own verb.
personal: What are you good at, albeit not as good as you'd like?
Who do you know who always helps, albeit with a lot of complaining?
hook: Albeit = 'all be it': all be it small, the flat is lovely.

intents: something that seemed like bad luck at first but turned out well
when missing your train leads to meeting the love of your life on the next one
a setback you later feel grateful for, because it led to something better
ru_cue: неудача, которая потом оказалась удачей
plain: a good thing in the end

upgrades.plain: Losing that job was [a good thing in the end]: I started my own business a month later.
upgrades.better: Losing that job was *a blessing in disguise*: I started my own business a month later.

upgrades.plain: Being dumped two weeks before the holiday felt awful, but it turned out to be [lucky after all].
upgrades.better: Being dumped two weeks before the holiday felt awful, but it turned out to be *a blessing in disguise*.

upgrades.plain: The power cut was [actually a good thing]; for once the whole family talked.
upgrades.better: The power cut was *a blessing in disguise*; for once the whole family talked.

collocations.chunk: turned out to be a blessing in disguise

collocations.frame: Getting rejected was ___: a better offer came a week later.

ru_trap: 'Нет худа без добра' is a whole saying; in English the idiom is a noun phrase: 'it was a blessing in disguise'.
nuance: Bad first, good later; a double-edged sword has a good and a bad side at the same time.
personal: What setback in your life turned out to be a blessing in disguise?
Has a friend ever lost a job or a partner, and it was a blessing in disguise?
hook: Picture a present wrapped in ugly brown paper: you sigh, open it, and it's exactly what you wanted.

intents: by its very nature, as a built-in part of what something is
when the danger comes from the activity itself, not from doing it badly, like climbing without ropes
describe a quality that belongs to the thing itself and can't be taken away
ru_cue: по самой своей природе, а не из-за обстоятельств

upgrades.plain: Climbing without ropes is [by its very nature] dangerous.
upgrades.better: Climbing without ropes is *inherently* dangerous.

upgrades.plain: There's nothing [in itself] wrong with changing your mind, Dad, so stop calling me a quitter.
upgrades.better: There's nothing *inherently* wrong with changing your mind, Dad, so stop calling me a quitter.

upgrades.plain: Some jobs are [just naturally] stressful, whatever the pay.
upgrades.better: Some jobs are *inherently* stressful, whatever the pay.

nuance: About what something is at its core; invariably is about how often (always), predominantly about how much (mostly).
personal: Is there an activity you think is inherently risky but still enjoy?
Do you know someone who is inherently calm, whatever happens?
hook: In-HERE-ntly: the quality is in here, built into the thing itself.

intents: mainly; for the most part, though not entirely
describing what most of a group or place is made up of: mostly young people, mostly farmland
when nearly all, but not every one, of something is of one kind
ru_cue: когда почти все в группе одного типа, кроме немногих

upgrades.plain: The audience was [mostly] students.
upgrades.better: The audience was *predominantly* students.

upgrades.plain: This region is [mainly] farmland.
upgrades.better: This region is *predominantly* farmland.

upgrades.plain: I was nervous on my first day because the team was [mostly] men twice my age.
upgrades.better: I was nervous on my first day because the team was *predominantly* men twice my age.

nuance: A formal 'mostly', used for what something is made up of; invariably means always, with no exceptions.
personal: Are your friends predominantly from school, from work, or from somewhere else?
What does your best friend predominantly spend money on?
hook: Pre-DOMINANT-ly: one kind dominates and makes up most of the crowd.

intents: always, every single time, with no exceptions
when something happens so reliably you could bet on it: every time I wash the car, it rains
a habit or result that never once changes
ru_cue: каждый раз, без единого исключения

upgrades.plain: He [always] arrives ten minutes early.
upgrades.better: He *invariably* arrives ten minutes early.

upgrades.plain: Plans made in a hurry [always] go wrong.
upgrades.better: Plans made in a hurry *invariably* go wrong.

upgrades.plain: Family dinners at my aunt's [always] end with my uncle and my dad shouting about money.
upgrades.better: Family dinners at my aunt's *invariably* end with my uncle and my dad shouting about money.

nuance: A slightly formal 'always', often for patterns you've noticed, especially annoying ones; predominantly means mostly, not always.
personal: What do you invariably forget when you pack for a trip?
What does someone in your family invariably say at dinner?
hook: In-VARI-ably: 'никаких вариантов', it's the same every single time.

intents: by accident, without meaning to, often causing a small problem
when you give away the surprise party because you forgot it was a secret
do something you never intended while you were busy doing something else
ru_cue: сделать что-то, не желая и даже не замечая этого

upgrades.plain: I [accidentally] deleted all my holiday photos while clearing space on my phone.
upgrades.better: I *inadvertently* deleted all my holiday photos while clearing space on my phone.

upgrades.plain: She [accidentally] gave away the surprise, and my mum's face fell.
upgrades.better: She *inadvertently* gave away the surprise, and my mum's face fell.

upgrades.plain: The email was [accidentally] sent to the whole office.
upgrades.better: The email was *inadvertently* sent to the whole office.

nuance: More formal than by accident, and usually about a side effect of doing something else: you didn't notice, rather than you slipped.
personal: What embarrassing thing have you once done inadvertently?
Has a friend ever inadvertently told you a secret about someone else?
hook: In-ADVERT-ently: you never meant to advertise the surprise, but you did.

intents: the small, visible part of a problem that is much bigger underneath
when one complaint turns out to be the first sign of hundreds more
what you can see now is nothing compared with what's hidden
ru_cue: то, что видно, лишь крошечная часть настоящей беды
plain: only a small part of it

upgrades.plain: The damp patch was [only a small part of the problem]; the whole wall had to come down.
upgrades.better: The damp patch was just *the tip of the iceberg*; the whole wall had to come down.

upgrades.plain: Those three complaints are [just the start]; hundreds more people are unhappy.
upgrades.better: Those three complaints are only *the tip of the iceberg*; hundreds more people are unhappy.

upgrades.plain: Their row about the dishes was [just a small sign of much bigger problems] in their marriage.
upgrades.better: Their row about the dishes was just *the tip of the iceberg* in their marriage.

collocations.chunk: only the tip of the iceberg
just the tip of the iceberg
collocations.frame: That's just ___; there's much worse to come.

ru_trap: Russian 'верхушка' tempts 'the top of the iceberg'; English says *the tip*.
nuance: Always about a bigger problem hidden behind a small one, so usually negative; 'just the start' has no sense of something hidden.
personal: Have you ever noticed a small problem that turned out to be the tip of the iceberg?
Has a friend ever mentioned one worry that was only the tip of the iceberg?
gesture: Hold one finger up just above a flat hand (the waterline), then sweep both arms wide below it to show the huge part underneath.
hook: Picture a ship's lookout seeing a tiny white point above the waves, and the giant mass of ice under it.

intents: in a way that seems contradictory or impossible, yet is true
the word to open a sentence like 'the more I rush in the morning, the later I leave', flagging that it works strangely back to front
the result is the opposite of what common sense predicts, strange as that is
ru_cue: вопреки ожиданиям и здравому смыслу, но это правда

upgrades.plain: [Strangely], adding more lanes often makes traffic worse.
upgrades.better: *Paradoxically*, adding more lanes often makes traffic worse.

upgrades.plain: [Oddly enough], the more I revised the night before, the worse I did, and I nearly failed the year.
upgrades.better: *Paradoxically*, the more I revised the night before, the worse I did, and I nearly failed the year.

upgrades.plain: Sleeping more can, [strangely], make you feel more tired at first.
upgrades.better: Sleeping more can, *paradoxically*, make you feel more tired at first.

collocations.frame: ___, the more choice people have, the less happy they are.
somewhat ___, the quietest students wrote the best essays

nuance: For a result that seems to contradict itself (less practice, better playing); ironically is for a result that mocks someone's intention.
personal: What paradoxically makes you more tired the more you do it?
Do you know someone who, paradoxically, gets calmer as things get more stressful?
hook: Sounds like 'пара доков': two doctors at the bedside, and the patient feels worse.

intents: very similar in nature to something else
when you compare one experience to another to explain it: talking to him is like talking to a wall
from the same family of feelings or things, though not identical
ru_cue: по сути очень похоже на что-то другое

upgrades.plain: Talking to my teenage son is [like] talking to a wall.
upgrades.better: Talking to my teenage son is *akin to* talking to a wall.

upgrades.plain: Learning chess is [similar to] learning a new language.
upgrades.better: Learning chess is *akin to* learning a new language.

upgrades.plain: The pain was [a bit like] a bad toothache.
upgrades.better: The pain was *akin to* a bad toothache.

collocations.frame: more ___ a hobby than a job

collocations.chunk: akin to talking to a wall

ru_trap: Russian 'сродни чему-то' needs no preposition; English always needs *to*: 'akin to fear', not 'akin fear' or 'akin with'.
nuance: More formal than like; it says two things share their nature, so it suits feelings, experiences and ideas rather than looks.
personal: What do you do that feels akin to meditation?
Who do you know whose job is akin to being a referee all day?
hook: Akin = 'a kin': like relatives, two things akin to each other look alike.

intents: seen absolutely everywhere, impossible to get away from
when you can't walk down a single street without seeing one, like coffee shops or phones
so common that it seems to be in every place at the same time
ru_cue: попадается на глаза буквально на каждом шагу

upgrades.plain: Coffee shops are [everywhere] now; there's one on every corner.
upgrades.better: Coffee shops are *ubiquitous* now; there's one on every corner.

upgrades.plain: That song was [everywhere] the summer I got dumped, so I couldn't escape it.
upgrades.better: That song was *ubiquitous* the summer I got dumped, so I couldn't escape it.

upgrades.plain: Smartphones are [in everyone's hands], even in tiny villages.
upgrades.better: Smartphones are *ubiquitous*, even in tiny villages.

nuance: Literally everywhere you look, usually things you can see; prevalent is about how common something is among people (an illness, a belief).
personal: What is ubiquitous in your city that you wish would disappear?
Which friend's catchphrase has become ubiquitous in your group?
gesture: Point quickly in every direction around you: there, there, there, everywhere.
hook: Sounds like 'у бика': у бика, у соседа, у бабушки, у каждого, it's simply everywhere.

intents: common among a particular group of people, or in a particular place or period
describing an illness, belief or habit that many people in a place share, like colds in winter
widespread enough to be a pattern, not just a few cases
ru_cue: широко встречается среди людей в каком-то месте или в какое-то время

upgrades.plain: Colds are much more [common] in winter.
upgrades.better: Colds are much more *prevalent* in winter.

upgrades.plain: Anxiety is [very common] among students in exam season, and that year I was one of them.
upgrades.better: Anxiety is highly *prevalent* among students in exam season, and that year I was one of them.

upgrades.plain: That kind of scam is [widespread] around the holidays.
upgrades.better: That kind of scam is *prevalent* around the holidays.

ru_trap: Russian 'превалирующий' means dominant; English *prevalent* just means widespread or common.
nuance: About how common something is in a population (diseases, beliefs, practices), often in formal writing; ubiquitous means visibly everywhere.
personal: What bad habit is most prevalent among people your age?
What attitude was prevalent when your parents were young?
hook: Prevalent sounds like 'превалирует': it's what you find in most people around.

intents: an advantage that can also turn against the person who has it
a tool or tactic, like advertising your business online, that brings success but can turn round and hurt you
a move that helps you but carries a built-in risk of backfiring on you
ru_cue: то, что помогает, но может ударить и по тебе самому

upgrades.plain: Lending money to friends [can help but can also backfire on you]: you might lose the money and the friend.
upgrades.better: Lending money to friends is *a double-edged sword*: you might lose the money and the friend.

upgrades.plain: Offering big discounts [brings in customers but can backfire]; we were packed all week, still lost money, and I had to tell my staff there'd be no bonus.
upgrades.better: Offering big discounts is *a double-edged sword*; we were packed all week, still lost money, and I had to tell my staff there'd be no bonus.

upgrades.plain: Cheap flights [help small islands but can also turn against them]: they bring money, but also crowds that damage them.
upgrades.better: Cheap flights are *a double-edged sword* for small islands: they bring money, but also crowds that damage them.

collocations.frame: Social media is ___ for small businesses.

ru_trap: Russian 'палка о двух концах' tempts 'a stick with two ends'; English says *a double-edged sword*.
nuance: The good and the bad come together, and the bad can hit the user; a blessing in disguise is bad first and good later.
personal: What in your life is a double-edged sword: a skill, a habit, a gadget?
Whose strong personality in your family is a double-edged sword?
gesture: Swing an imaginary sword forward, then wince as the back edge 'cuts' your own shoulder.
hook: Picture a blade sharp on both sides: swing it at a problem and the back edge nicks your own arm.

intents: harmful to something such as your health, sleep or reputation
when a habit like skipping breakfast quietly does real harm to your health
describing an effect that damages something rather than helping it
ru_cue: плохо сказывается на чем-то, наносит ущерб

upgrades.plain: Too much screen time is [bad for] your sleep.
upgrades.better: Too much screen time is *detrimental* to your sleep.

upgrades.plain: The scandal was [really bad for] his reputation, and he lost half his clients.
upgrades.better: The scandal was seriously *detrimental* to his reputation, and he lost half his clients.

upgrades.plain: My dad keeps telling me that night shifts are [harmful to] my health, and we argue about it every Sunday.
upgrades.better: My dad keeps telling me that night shifts are *detrimental* to my health, and we argue about it every Sunday.

ru_trap: Russian 'вредный для' tempts 'detrimental for'; English says detrimental *to* (or 'a detrimental effect on').
nuance: A formal word for harmful, used of effects (on health, morale, the environment); exacerbate is a verb for making an existing problem worse.
personal: Which of your habits is most detrimental to your sleep?
What does someone in your family do that you think is detrimental to their health?
hook: Detri-MENTAL sounds like 'debt-ri-mental': debts are bad for your mental health.
